instruction: Scorpius, October, 19°lat, medium light pollution. 20-second whisper.
output: Face south. Antares burns red at the scorpion's heart. Trace right to Sargas, then down to Shaula's twin sting. Scorpius once guarded the harvest; sailors steered by its tail. Breathe. The city glow eats the claws — the heart stays.

Look south-east. Three belt stars — Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka — a straight short line. Above left glows red Betelgeuse; below right burns blue Rigel. Hunters saw a guardian here; you are seeing a stellar nursery 1,300 light years out. Let your eyes rest soft.

Look north-east, high up. Seven dipper stars from Dubhe to Alkaid pour a long ladle. Follow the two pointer stars away from the cup to find Polaris. Bears, wagons, ploughs — every culture drew a traveler here. You are under the same road.

Small, bright, almost overhead. Acrux at the foot, Gacrux at the head, Mimosa to the side — the Southern Cross fits behind your thumb. It points south when the pole star is gone. Navigators trusted this kite of four. You can too.
Face north. One steady star halfway up — Kochab nearby, the rest wheeling around it. That is Polaris, less than a degree from true north. Everything else turns; it holds. If you are lost, start here.

Straight up, the brightest white spark — Vega. It once defined magnitude zero; every star is measured against it. Summer triangles hang off it. Stand still. The monsoon haze will part for seconds at a time.

Low in the south-east, flashing colors — that is Sirius, the brightest star, doubled by our own air. Egyptians timed the Nile by it. Do not chase the colors; they are the atmosphere shivering, not the star.
One red ember through the cloud gap — Antares, heart of the scorpion. Armies called it the rival of Mars. Hold the moment; the clouds keep the rest tonight, and one true star is enough.

instruction: Milky Way band, October, dark site. 20-second whisper.
output: Let your eyes go wide. The pale river overhead is our galaxy edge-on — billions of suns too far to separate. Deneb swims at one end. No myth covers it; it is too big for stories. Just listen to the dark between stars.

instruction: New moon, city terrace, first-timer. 20-second whisper.
output: Start with the brightest thing you see — that is a planet or Sirius playing tricks. Wait ten minutes without your phone. The second-brightest things are the real guides: Betelgeuse red, Rigel blue. Night vision is a slow sense. Give it time.

instruction: Kids group, Orion, winter camp. 20-second whisper.
output: Find the three belt buttons in a row — Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka. Hang a sword down from the middle; that fuzzy star is a whole nursery of baby suns. The hunter Orion got stung by Scorpius, so they chase each other forever. Who is winning tonight?

instruction: Light-polluted balcony, only 5 stars visible. 20-second whisper.
output: Five stars is plenty. Name them by color: red Betelgeuse, blue Rigel, white Sirius. Pollution hides the faint ones but the bright ones punch through — they guided ships through worse haze. Pocket the phone, keep the five.
